Hook: In 2006 two economists, Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier, published the attendance records of 7,752 members of three American health clubs, over three years. Many members bought a monthly contract, for over 70 dollars a month, with unlimited visits. They then went, on average, 4.3 times a month. Each visit cost them over 17 dollars. The same clubs sold a ten-visit pass, at 10 dollars a visit. The members would have paid less, for the same visits, with the pass. They were paying not to go to the gym.

The Island has a gym too, with the same two prices. When members sign up, they forecast how often they will go: each dot is a monthly member, with the forecast across and the visits made up the side. If people went as often as they planned, the dots would sit on the dashed line. On average, monthly members expect 13.9 visits a month. They make 4.7. So they pay 15 dollars 02 a visit, and 84 percent of them would have done better with the pass. Nobody here is short of information, or bad at arithmetic. They are wrong about something else: their own future selves.

So this part asks what changes in economics when people are not the agents of Part five, who knew what they wanted and chose it. Which of those assumptions fail, and how would we know? How do economists measure a bias in real decisions, not only in the laboratory? What do markets, and the firms in them, do with people's biases? And if choices are not always in people's interest, what does it mean to make someone better off?
Economics, Built. Part forty-five: behavioural economics.

Here is the plan. Three ways people depart from the textbook, a mug for you to sell, and reference points, in the laboratory and in marathons, golf and housing. Present bias, the difference between knowing it and not, what people do to bind themselves, and the power of defaults. Inattention, fairness, and whether markets cure biases or feed on them. What welfare means when choices conflict, what nudges do at scale, and models of minds with limits. Three dials, the people who use these ideas, and the frontier.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: your mug.

Your turn. Here is a mug from the Island's gift shop, and it is yours to keep. Before you take it home, someone offers to buy it. What is the lowest price at which you would sell it? Not what you think it is worth to others: the price at which you would rather have the money than the mug. In the next room, people who were not given a mug are asked the mirror question: the most they would pay for one. Pause, and write down your price.

Here is one session on the Island: 44 people, 22 of them given a mug at random. In blue, the buyers' bids, highest first. If owners valued the mug just as buyers do, their asks would be the dashed line, and every mug whose owner values it less than some buyer would change hands: here 10 of 22, close to half, as the Coase theorem of Part fifteen predicts when trading is free. But the Island's owners feel giving up the mug as a loss, and losses count 2 times as much as gains, so every ask doubles. Now bids beat asks for only 5 mugs. Nothing about the mugs or the people changed, only who happened to be holding one.

Run the session 4,000 times. Without loss aversion, half the mugs change hands on average. With it, 24 percent do. The median owner asks 8 dollars 07, the median buyer bids 4 dollars 03. In 1990 Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler ran this experiment with real coffee mugs and real money. Owners asked about twice what buyers would pay, and far fewer mugs traded than the half that standard theory predicts. They called it the endowment effect. Compare your own price with what you would have paid.
Reference: The mug market is prospect theory at work, the theory of choice that Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published in 1979. Outcomes are felt as gains or losses against a reference point, here what you already hold, not as levels of wealth. Each additional dollar of gain feels a little less than the last, and so does each additional dollar of loss. And losses loom larger: with the parameters Tversky and Kahneman estimated in 1992, losing fifty dollars feels like minus 70, winning fifty like 31. The ratio, lambda, is two and a quarter. An owner who sells a mug loses the mug; a buyer gains it. That asymmetry is the gap between asks and bids. The theory also weights small probabilities too heavily, the story of Part twenty-six of Psychology, Built; this part needs only the kink at the reference point.

Is the endowment effect a fixed trait, or does it fade with practice? The Island assumes it fades: a trader's loss aversion over goods bought to be sold again halves every five trades. Newcomers trade only 25 percent of the goods that should change hands. Veterans trade about half, as standard theory says. That is an assumption. Whether it holds is a question for data, and John List went to find out.

At a trading-card show in Orlando, Florida, in 1998, List gave each of 148 traders one of two collectibles of about the same market value: a ticket stub from the game in which Cal Ripken set the record for consecutive games, or a souvenir of Nolan Ryan's three-hundredth win. Then he offered each trader the other one in exchange. Which good a trader got was random, so without an endowment effect about half should swap. Only 34 percent did. But sort the traders by how often they trade: those who never trade almost never swapped, 19 percent of those making one to four trades a month did, and about half of those making ten or more. Among traders who are not dealers, 7 percent of the occasional ones swapped, against 47 percent of the regulars. Experience teaches people out of the anomaly, at least for goods they handle often. Whether it does the same for a pension, chosen once in a lifetime, is another question.

Everything depends on where the reference point sits. Sometimes it is what you hold. Sometimes the status quo: your current plan, your current job, last year's price. Sometimes a goal: a finishing time, par on a golf hole, the price you paid for a flat. Botond Koszegi and Matthew Rabin proposed that it is what you recently expected to happen. A theory that lets the reference point be anything can explain anything, so the test is to fix it in advance and check the predictions, which is what the next chapter does with goals.
Field: Chapter four. In the field: runners, golfers, sellers.

Laboratory mugs are cheap. Does reference dependence survive when the stakes are hours of training? Here are the finishing times of 400 thousand marathon runners on the Island, minute by minute. Look just before each half hour: three hours, three and a half, four. Too many runners finish there. And just after, too few. Eric Allen, Patricia Dechow, Devin Pope and George Wu found exactly this shape in nearly ten million real marathon finishing times: runners bunch just under round numbers, most visibly under three and four hours. Nothing about running changes at four hours. Only the goal does.

Why the shape? On the Island each runner chooses effort, which is costly. A minute saved is worth something, plus a gain-loss term around the goal: below four hours each minute is a gain, above it each minute is a loss, and losses count lambda times more. So the reward for speed jumps at the goal: a kink, like the jump in a tax rate in Part forty-one. Runners whose natural time lies just over the goal push to just under it. Fit a smooth curve to the histogram away from the goal, as Part forty-one did for taxpayers. The excess under four hours is about 1.9 minutes' worth of runners, and about as many are missing just over it. The planted kink moves 2.5 minutes' worth of runners onto the goal; the estimator recovers most of it. The size of the bunch is a measure of how much losses outweigh gains.

Golf has a reference point printed on the card: par. A putt for par avoids a loss; a putt for birdie, one under par, is a gain. On the Island, the share of putts holed falls steeply with length, for both kinds. And birdie putts are longer on average, because they usually follow an approach shot, while a par putt often follows a missed birdie putt or a chip. So comparing all par putts with all birdie putts gives a gap of 21 percentage points, which is mostly distance: the selection problem of Part four, where the comparison groups differ in more than the thing being studied.

So compare putts of the same length. Each bar is the difference between par and birdie putts within one band of distance. At almost every length, par putts go in a little more often. Averaged, the gap is 2.2 points, close to the planted 2.5. Devin Pope and Maurice Schweitzer did this with millions of laser-measured putts on the PGA Tour. Professionals, with large sums at stake and years of practice, hole par putts about two percentage points more often than birdie putts of the same length: they try harder to avoid a loss than to secure a gain.

The last test has the largest stakes: selling a home. After flat prices fall, many owners face a loss against the price they paid. On the Island, a loss-averse owner asks the flat's value plus 0.3 of the nominal loss. Each dot is a group of owners, by the size of their loss. The econometrician never sees a flat's value, only its features, and a flat that is better than its features is both bought for more, which looks like a bigger loss, and listed for more. Ignore that, and the estimate is 0.68: too high. Control for how far the last sale price stood above the features' value, and the estimate falls to 0.27: too low, because that residual also contains the owner's luck when buying. The two estimates bracket the truth. And the owners with losses, asking more, wait 20 weeks to sell instead of 11. David Genesove and Christopher Mayer found this in downtown Boston's condominium market from 1990 to 1997: owners facing a nominal loss asked more, by a quarter to a third of the gap between the expected price and the price they had paid, got more, and sold more slowly.
Present: Part seven discounted the future at a steady rate: each day further away is worth the same fraction less. That is the grey curve. Present bias adds one number. Everything that is not today is multiplied by beta, less than one, and after that the steady rate applies. The formula is due to Edmund Phelps and Robert Pollak, and David Laibson brought it into economics in 1997. The whole difference is a drop between now and everything else. Between next Tuesday and next Wednesday, nothing special happens. Between today and tomorrow, a great deal does.

The drop makes plans unstable. Offer a hundred dollars today or a hundred and ten tomorrow. Tomorrow's money is cut by beta, so the hundred and ten feels like 77: take the hundred today. Now offer the same pair a year from now: a hundred in a year, or a hundred and ten in a year and a day. Both are in the future, both are cut by beta, and the extra ten dollars wins. So today you plan to wait for the hundred and ten. A year from now, the day arrives, the first option becomes today, and you take the hundred. Your plan and your choice disagree, and they will disagree every time. The gym member signs up as the planner and shows up, or not, as the chooser.

Ted O'Donoghue and Matthew Rabin asked what happens when people do, or do not, know they are present biased. Take a report due within four weeks, with beta one half. Writing it costs 3 this week, then 5, 8 and 13 as other work piles up. Part five's agent writes it in week 1. The naif, sure that a later self will do it, keeps postponing to a week that looks cheap from today, and writes it in week 4, at the worst cost. The sophisticate knows the week-three self would also postpone, so week two is the last chance before the worst week, and writes it in week 2. Knowing your bias helps. Now a pleasure instead: a film, better each week, 3, 5, 8, 13. Part five's agent waits for the best, week 4. The naif gives in early, in week 3. The sophisticate, expecting to give in anyway, gives in in week 1. Knowing your bias, with pleasures, can make it worse.

Now be the gym. What contract should you offer a present-biased member? Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier worked it out in 2004. For a good whose costs come now and benefits later, the profit-maximizing price of a visit is below what a visit costs the gym, by the share of the benefit the member's present bias throws away. On the Island, a visit costs the gym 3 dollars, and the best price is minus 4.20. Below zero. The fee carries the profit. A monopoly gym charges the naif a higher fee than the sophisticate, because the naif expects to go more often, and leaves the naif worse off than staying home, by 12 dollars 96. Competition returns the fee to cost for both. The per-visit price stays below cost: for a present-biased member, that helps, a little commitment sold with the membership. Real gyms cannot pay people to come, so the price of a visit stops at zero: a flat fee with free visits, the contract of the hook.
Commitment: Here is a sharp test. The agent of Part five never pays to give up an option. An option it does not want, it simply does not use. But a sophisticate, who knows tomorrow's self will be tempted, may want to bind that self in advance, like Ulysses, who had his crew tie him to the mast before the sirens began to sing. In money, that is an account you cannot touch until a date, or until a goal is reached, even though it pays no more interest than an ordinary one. So if people choose such an account, the choice itself is evidence: of present bias, and of knowing it.

Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan and Wesley Yin ran the test with a rural bank on Mindanao, in the Philippines. The bank's clients were surveyed first, including questions that revealed whether they were patient for the far future but impatient for the near one. Then some of them, chosen at random, were offered a new account: money deposited could not be withdrawn until a date or an amount the client set, and it earned no extra interest. Of the 710 clients offered it, 202, twenty-eight percent, took it, and women whose survey answers showed the tell-tale reversal were more likely to. A year later, the average savings balance of those offered the account had risen by 81 percentage points more than that of those not offered. Commitment was demanded, and it worked.

The Island runs the same trial, with 1,800 clients. Of those offered the locked account, 30 percent take it. Comparing everyone offered with everyone not offered, savings are 11.0 points higher: the effect of the offer, which randomization makes clean. Only the takers can have been changed by the account, so the effect on a taker is the effect of the offer divided by the take-up: 36 points, the Wald ratio of Part four. And the takers are the more present-biased, with an average beta of 0.64 against 0.72. They are mostly sophisticates. Naifs, sure they will save anyway, see no use for a lock, which is why the people who might need commitment most are the least likely to ask for it.
Defaults: In 2001 Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea studied a large American company that changed one thing in its retirement plan. Before, new employees had to sign up to join. After, new employees were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out. The plan, the employer's matching contribution and the investment choices were the same. Participation among new hires jumped, from 37 percent to 86 percent, as the authors later summarized it. And many of the new participants stayed exactly at the default: its low contribution rate and its conservative fund, which few had chosen before. For the agent of Part five, which box is ticked when you arrive should not matter. It matters enormously.

The Island's new hires each have an ideal saving rate, zero for a few. Changing the rate takes an afternoon of forms, a cost paid now, while the gain comes over decades. For Part five's workers the default barely matters: within weeks nearly everyone is at their ideal rate, whichever box was ticked. Present-biased naifs are another story. Signing up always looks better next month. A year in, 63 percent of them save when they must sign up, and 98 percent when they are enrolled automatically. And after three years, 36 percent are still at the default rate, whatever their ideal. The default decides because the decision is put off.

Why do defaults stick? The Island's answer is procrastination. Acting now costs the effort k now; waiting a month costs one month's gain g. A naif, believing next month's self will act, compares the two with the present cut by beta, and with a beta of 0.7 that means acting only when the effort is a small fraction of what a time-consistent worker would bear. In real plans, a default also reads as advice: the employer must think this is sensible. And it becomes the reference point, so leaving it feels like a loss. Whatever the reason, there is no neutral design. Some box is always ticked. Gabriel Carroll, James Choi, David Laibson, Brigitte Madrian and Andrew Metrick showed how to choose it: a default works well when people's needs are alike, and requiring an active choice works better when needs differ widely and people are prone to put decisions off.

If biases can block saving, can they be turned around to help it? Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed Save More Tomorrow: workers commit today to put part of each future pay rise into saving. The design uses present bias, since the cost comes later, and loss aversion, since take-home pay never falls; and inertia then keeps people in. On the Island, only 4 percent would raise their saving now, but 69 percent sign up to raise it later, and with four rises their rate climbs from 3.5 to 15 percent. In the first company to use it, 78 percent of those offered the plan joined, and their average saving rate rose from three and a half percent to thirteen point six percent over forty months.
Inattention: Some prices are on the tag; others arrive later. A printer, then its ink. A hotel room, then its minibar. A bank account, then its overdraft fee. On the Island, most buyers of printers do not think about ink when they buy; it costs 3 dollars to make and sells for 18. Competition does not drive the ink's price down, because nobody chooses a printer by it. It drives the printer's price down instead, to 9 dollars 50, below its cost of 20 dollars, paid for by the ink. Myopic buyers pay 27 dollars 50 in all. Sophisticated buyers take the cheap printer and avoid the dear ink, refilling cartridges or printing elsewhere, and pay 15 dollars 50. In a competitive market the inattentive subsidize the attentive. Xavier Gabaix and David Laibson called these shrouded attributes.

Why does no firm advertise the truth about ink and steal the customers? Suppose a firm does. The myopes it educates become sophisticates. But a sophisticate does not need the honest firm: the cheapest move is to buy any firm's subsidized printer and avoid its ink. The firm that revealed the shroud gains nobody, and pays for the advertising. So in equilibrium no firm unshrouds, even in a competitive market. Gabaix and Laibson called it the curse of debiasing.

Inattention leaves fingerprints in prices. Here are wholesale prices of used cars on the Island, by mileage, from 400 thousand sales. Each dot averages the cars in a five-hundred-mile bin. More miles, lower price, as it should be. Take away the straight-line trend, and a sawtooth appears: at every ten thousand miles the price drops by a step, as if 49,999 miles and 50,000 were very different cars, by about 171 dollars. Buyers here read the first digit fully and only part of the rest. If theta is the share of the remaining digits they ignore, the step and the slope between steps pin it down: theta is the step divided by the step plus ten thousand miles' worth of slope. The estimate is 0.28, against a planted 0.3. Nicola Lacetera, Devin Pope and Justin Sydnor found these steps in more than 22 million real wholesale car sales, drops of roughly 150 to 200 dollars at each ten-thousand-mile mark. The buyers at those auctions are professional dealers; the evidence fits partial inattention by the retail customers they sell to, whose bias the dealers pass back into wholesale prices.
Social: In the ultimatum game one player proposes how to split a pie, and the other accepts, or rejects and both get nothing. Part five's agents would offer a crumb, and it would be accepted. In laboratories around the world, offers are much more generous than that, and low offers are often rejected. Ernst Fehr and Klaus Schmidt explained this with one change to the agent: people dislike inequality. Alpha measures how much it hurts to have less than the other player, beta how much it hurts to have more. A responder with envy alpha prefers nothing to an offer below alpha over one plus two alpha. On the Island, envy varies from person to person, and this is the share who would accept each offer. 51 percent would turn down a fifth of the pie. Proposers who know this offer a lot: on average 44 percent, and those whose guilt beta exceeds a half offer exactly half, because for them every dollar of advantage hurts more than it pleases.

If workers reciprocate kindness, an employer might pay more than it must and get more effort back: the gift exchange behind efficiency wages in Part thirty-eight. Laboratory experiments find it. Does it survive a real job? Uri Gneezy and John List hired people for one-day jobs, entering library books into a database and raising money door to door. On arrival, some were told they would be paid more than advertised. They worked harder at first, but within a few hours the difference was gone. The Island's workers are built the same way. Reciprocity is real, but it can be shorter-lived in the field than in the laboratory, where most sessions last an hour.

The simplest measure of generosity is the dictator game. One player divides a sum of money with an anonymous other, who has no say at all. Most dictators give something, which looked like direct evidence of altruism. John List changed the menu: dictators could also take money from the other player. Giving fell sharply, and many took. If dictators had fixed preferences over the two payoffs, adding options they did not use should not have changed what they chose. So the game measures preferences, but also what the menu suggests is appropriate, and the sense of being watched. Social motives also interact with incentives. In Part one, a fine for late pickup at six Israeli day-care centres was followed by more late parents, not fewer: a fine is a price. A 2020 replication that put the same situation to online respondents as a written scenario found the opposite, fines reducing intended lateness. A survey is not a field experiment, but one striking result should be held as what it is: one result.
Welfare: Welfare economics, from Part nine to Part forty-two, measured well-being by choices: what you choose is what you prefer. Behavioural economics breaks that link. Take a worker who never joins a pension plan when joining means signing up, as if joining were worth less than an afternoon of forms, say 30 dollars. Enrolled automatically, the same worker stays in, as if joining were worth more than 80. Which choice reveals what this worker wants? Douglas Bernheim and Antonio Rangel proposed an answer: when choices conflict across frames that should not matter, trust only what they agree on. The worker's value of joining is somewhere between 30 and 80. A policy that costs the worker less than 30 makes them better off whichever frame you believe. One that costs more than 80 makes them worse off. In between, the choices do not say, and the economist should admit it.

Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein turned this into a policy philosophy they called libertarian paternalism, and popularized as nudging. Some default, some menu, some order is unavoidable, so choose them to help people, as judged by themselves, while keeping every option open and cheap to take. The objections are serious. Who decides what helps? The designer may be wrong, or have interests of its own. The same tools sell as easily as they help: Thaler's own word for frictions that keep people from what they want is sludge, like the subscription that takes one click to start and an hour to cancel. And a cheap nudge can become an excuse not to change prices, rules or institutions, where most of the leverage is.

The Island can test a rule that respects choice. The gym must tell each would-be member how often members like them actually go. If no naif believes it, nothing changes: members gain 14 dollars 32 a month on average from the gym, after paying for it. If half of them believe it, 20 dollars 28. If all do, 26 dollars 25, and the share on monthly contracts falls from 60 to 9 percent. No contract was banned and nobody was told what to buy. The gain comes from better forecasts. But it depends entirely on whether people take the number to apply to them, and naifs, by definition, think they are the exception.
Scale: Governments set up nudge units to put these ideas to work: reminder letters, simpler forms, changed defaults, each tested in a randomized trial. How well do they work? In the academic journals, the average nudge raised take-up of the encouraged action by 8.7 percentage points. Stefano DellaVigna and Elizabeth Linos obtained every trial run by two large American nudge units: 126 trials involving about 23 million people. The average effect was 1.4 points: real and statistically clear, but six times smaller. The authors estimate that about 70 percent of the gap comes from selective publication, made worse by small samples; most of the rest from differences in the nudges themselves.

The Island shows how the filter works. Every nudge here truly raises take-up by 1.4 points on average. Researchers run 600 small trials, and a journal publishes the ones that are statistically significant, plus one in ten of the rest. Each gold dot is a published trial: its estimate across, its standard error up the side, so small trials sit high. The red line is the edge of significance. The published mean is 2.7, nearly double the truth: small trials only clear the bar when luck pushes their estimates up. A unit that reports all 150 of its larger trials gets 1.4. Nobody cheated. The filter alone did it: the winner's curse, which Part fifty-six of Statistics, Built treats as inference on winners, and the same arithmetic that inflates any literature that publishes by significance.

Can the filter be undone from the published trials alone? Isaiah Andrews and Maximilian Kasy's approach: model the filter. Each true effect is drawn around mu; each estimate around its true effect; and an estimate is published for sure if significant, with probability gamma if not. The likelihood of what was published divides by the chance of being published. The naive average is 2.67. The selection model estimates 1.19, and a publication chance for insignificant trials of 0.11. The truth is 1.4 and 0.1. The correction is not perfect, and it rests on the model of the filter being right, but it moves most of the way back.
Limits: A critic might say behavioural economics is a list of exceptions. Its most ambitious work tries to model limited minds as precisely as Part five modelled perfect ones. Christopher Sims proposed rational inattention: information is free to look at but costly to absorb, so people choose how much to learn, paying lambda for each unit of information. Filip Matejka and Alisdair McKay showed that the resulting choices follow a logit, tilted toward options that are often good. On the Island a shopper chooses between a familiar product and a new one whose value is uncertain. When attention is cheap, the shopper chooses the new product almost exactly when it is better. As attention gets dearer, the curve flattens: choices barely respond to what is at stake. And when the new product is usually worse, a shopper facing dear attention can rationally never look at it at all. Inattention, on this view, is a choice.

Xavier Gabaix proposed a related idea: sparsity. A decision maker starts from a simple default model of the world and pays attention to each feature only in proportion to how much it matters, minus a fixed cost kappa. Attention to a feature is one minus kappa over its importance, but never below zero. A car buyer weighs the price almost fully, quality somewhat, running costs less, and resale value and warranty terms not at all. The result is a model with exact zeros, like the lasso of Statistics, Built: small things are ignored completely, which is what left-digit bias and shrouded fees look like from the inside.

Limits also shape expectations, the subject of Part twenty-eight. Olivier Coibion and Yuriy Gorodnichenko's test regresses the error in a forecast on the revision that produced it. If forecasters use their information well, revisions should not predict errors. A positive slope means forecasts move too little when news arrives; a negative slope, too much. On the Island, forty forecasters each see the economy through private noise. When they are rational, each one's slope is minus 0.04, about zero, but the average forecast's slope is 1.17: the consensus under-reacts, because each person's news reaches the average only gradually. Now make them diagnostic, in the sense of Pedro Bordalo, Nicola Gennaioli and Andrei Shleifer: news that makes a state more likely than before makes it seem much more likely. Each forecaster now over-reacts, with a slope of minus 0.36, while the average still under-reacts, at 0.37. That is the pattern Bordalo, Gennaioli, Yueran Ma and Shleifer found in professional forecasts: individuals over-react, the consensus under-reacts. One model, two facts.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: structural behavioural economics, and behavioural macroeconomics.

Four frontiers. Structural behavioural economics. A treatment effect says what a nudge did; it does not say whether people are better off, or what a different policy would do. For that, estimate the parameters, the beta, the lambda, the cost of attention, from field choices, and use the model to predict. Stefano DellaVigna has argued that this is how behavioural findings become tools for policy. Behavioural macroeconomics. In Part thirty, promises about interest rates far in the future had implausibly large effects today, the forward-guidance puzzle. Xavier Gabaix showed that if households and firms discount the distant future through limited attention, the puzzle shrinks. Theories learned from data. With thousands of choices, a flexible learner can find the best fit that is achievable at all, and a theory can be graded by how close it comes. Psychology, Built ran this race for prospect theory on thirteen thousand gamble problems. And robustness. Some famous findings, like ego depletion, did not survive large, preregistered replications; others, like loss aversion in many settings and the power of defaults, did, at sizes that are now being pinned down.

Here is one result from that race, refitted for this part. Joshua Peterson and his coauthors collected online choices between pairs of gambles on an unprecedented scale. Fitting prospect theory to 1,928 of the problems described in words, with 31,700 choices, against Tversky and Kahneman's parameters in grey, gives a loss aversion of 1.13, in gold, not 2.25. In these risky choices between gambles the kink is far smaller. Loss aversion is not one number; the first dial, in chapter fourteen, collected what it is in different settings.
